message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"3.25","text":"Therefore she imposed an equivocal name on her firstborn, calling him Cain, which admits a twofold interpretation; for it is interpreted both as “possession” and as “jealousy,” since in what was to come he was going to be jealous of either a wife or possessions or the parents’ affection toward him. But if none of these things actually came about, even so, calling him “possession” has hit the mark well; for she acquired him first, and this also proved useful to her. For he was a “murderer,” “and a liar,” and, amid sins, was unwilling to live quietly even while ruling. Moreover, those who came from his line became the first adulterers; they fashioned psalteries and lyres and became bronzesmiths of weapons of war. Therefore, how the prophecy of the descendants too, full of adulterers and psalteries, secretly stirs up wars through sensual pleasures!","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἀμφοτερίζον ἐπέθηκεν ὄνομα","chosen":"she imposed an equivocal name","rationale":"ἀμφοτερίζον describes a name that goes in both directions or bears two senses, as the following clause explains."},{"source_quote":"ὃ διχῇ ἔχει τῆς ἑρμηνείας τὴν ἐκδοχήν","chosen":"which admits a twofold interpretation","rationale":"The expression describes two possible outcomes or explanations of the name’s interpretation."},{"source_quote":"ὡς ζηλοῦν αὐτοῦ μέλλοντος ἐν τοῖς ἐσομένοις ἢ γυναῖκα ἢ κτήματα ἢ τὴν τῶν γονέων πρὸς αὐτὸν στοργήν","chosen":"since in what was to come he was going to be jealous of either a wife or possessions or the parents’ affection toward him","rationale":"The main rendering takes ὡς with the genitive absolute as an explanatory causal ground. Alternatively, ὡς may attribute an assumed reason to the namer: “on the assumption that in the future he would be jealous of either a wife or possessions or the parents’ affection toward him.” The following condition, εἰ δ’ ἄρα μηδὲν τούτων γένηται, leaves the anticipated jealousy contingent, so “was going to” avoids implying necessary fulfillment. αὐτοῦ is the subject of μέλλοντος, while the later αὐτόν may refer to Cain or to another contextually implied male; “toward him” preserves that referential uncertainty."},{"source_quote":"τὸ „κτῆμα“ λέγεσθαι καλῶς ἐπιτέτευκται","chosen":"calling him “possession” has hit the mark well","rationale":"ἐπιτυγχάνω conveys attaining or hitting the mark; the infinitive phrase functions as the subject."},{"source_quote":"„φονεὺς“ γὰρ ἦν „καὶ ψεύστης“","chosen":"For he was a “murderer,” “and a liar,”","rationale":"Keeps καὶ within the second quoted expression, following the source’s quotation boundaries rather than placing “and” outside the quotation."},{"source_quote":"μετὰ ἁμαρτιῶν ἡσυχάζειν μηδὲ ἐπὶ τῷ ἄρχειν θέλων","chosen":"amid sins, was unwilling to live quietly even while ruling","rationale":"Takes μετά as accompaniment or surrounding circumstance and ἐπὶ τῷ ἄρχειν temporally. Alternatives include “unwilling to rest with his sins, even in ruling” or taking the final phrase as “even for the sake of ruling.”"},{"source_quote":"ψαλτήρια καὶ κιθάρας ἡρμόσαντο","chosen":"they fashioned psalteries and lyres","rationale":"ἁρμόζω can mean fitting together, constructing, or tuning. “Fashioned” fits the account of originating instruments, while “tuned” remains possible."},{"source_quote":"χαλκεῖς ὅπλων πολεμικῶν ἐγένοντο","chosen":"became bronzesmiths of weapons of war","rationale":"χαλκεῖς specifically denotes workers in copper or bronze and, more broadly, metalworkers; the genitive identifies their products as weapons used in war."},{"source_quote":"λανθανόντως διὰ τῶν ἡδυπαθειῶν ὡς τοὺς πολέμους ἐγείρει","chosen":"how ... secretly stirs up wars through sensual pleasures!","rationale":"Takes ὡς before the finite clause as exclamatory, “how,” while λανθανόντως indicates that the effect operates unnoticed or secretly. A declarative reading such as “that it secretly stirs up wars” is also possible."}],"source_issues":[]}]}
